newsitem.title: UK: UK boosts security in case of IRA polling day bid.
newsitem.headline: UK boosts security in case of IRA polling day bid.

text.p: Britons going to vote in Thursday's general election are likely to find their polling stations surrounded by police on guard against the threat of Irish Republican Army (IRA) attacks.
A recent spate of IRA activity has brought chaos to Britain and raised fears that the guerrillas are planning to try to disrupt the election.
Main airports and motorways around London and in southern England were closed on Tuesday morning in a fresh spate of bomb alerts designed to snarl up commuter traffic.
The level of anxiety became clear last week when the Home Office (interior ministry) sent an unprecedented memo to polling station managers, telling them how to deal with possible bomb threats.
"Provided that an adequate security plan, based on police advice, has been put in place, it should be possible to avoid major disruption," the Home Office document said.

But if there is a bomb, or a threat which forces the polling station to be closed for a "substantial period of time", voting for that district may have to be postponed until the following day, it said.

This would pose tricky problems for polling station managers who would have to zealously guard the big black ballot boxes -- assuming police allowed them to take them from the building -- and make sure that nobody voted for a second time the next day.
Newspaper reports say voters could face searches and bag checks and police are certain to carry out meticulous searches of polling stations for hidden IRA bombs.
"There will be loads of police around. We are not going to put any of our people at risk," said one polling station manager.
Police refuse to discuss security arrangements, but they have made clear they fear an IRA attack on polling day.

"The election was always in the forefront of our minds as an opportunity likely to be exploited by the IRA ... It presents a significant security challenge, as current events are demonstrating," said David Veness, Assistant Commissioner of London's Metropolitan police.

Recent IRA activity in mainland Britain appears to have been designed to cause the utmost disruption -- bringing London to a virtual standstill on one day and cutting off the routes between north and south England on another -- without loss of life.

But on the day after the 1992 election, the IRA marked Prime Minister John Major's victory by bombing the Baltic Exchange international shipping market in London's financial district, killing three people and injuring 91.
Several people have been killed since then in the IRA's guerrilla war to end Britain's rule of Northern Ireland.

And though the opposition Labour Party, tipped by opinion polls to easily win the election, says that it will be no softer on the IRA than Major's Conservatives, the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein has said it would prefer a Labour victory.
